utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We are starting with cross-examination by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Savic. My name is David Re. I'm from the Prosecution and I'm going to ask you some questions about your testimony over the last couple of days. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to try and ask you some fairly precise questions about things and be very grateful if you could listen exactly to the question and try and confine yourself as much as possible to the question and answer that one.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for all of us here. Now, sir, you gave some evidence a couple of days ago to Mr. Pisarevic about your career. Essentially you spoke about being in the JNA and being an army officer in the VRS, I think since 1992. I just want to fill in a few details for the Trial Chamber, if possible. Your evidence was that you had been a reserve officer for many years up until the end of 1991, beginning of 1992. You were a reserve officer. What was your job, what was your career, what were you doing when you weren't being a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon completion of the reserve officer school in Bileca -- I got a job in the municipal Secretariat for National Defence in the municipality of Bosanski Samac. That's what it was called. I worked there for five years and at the same time, I was assigned to the war unit in Derventa. After five and a half or six years of my work at the Secretariat, I went to work as a commercial representative, as a travelling salesman but all the time I worked as the -- in the war unit in Derventa, and I was commander of the company, of the battalion, in various functions. This was up to 1991. From 1991 I still continued to be in the reserves, all the way until -- up until 1997. So I'm talking of my functions as a reserve officer. In 1996 [As interpreted], I went to the professional -- I was accepted into the professional military service, upon my request, so now I have become an officer of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one small correction for the transcript, on page 2, line 18, he said in 1997, he joined the professional army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, you heard what Mr. Lazarevic just said. The transcript says 1997. What year did you join the -- what year were you accepted as a -- I'm sorry, what year did you join the professional army? That's what I'm just trying to find out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So until 1991, beginning of 1992, the years immediately before then, you'd been working as a commercial salesman or salesperson. You then were in the reserves, had a full-time job, was it a full-time job in the army from then onwards? That's what I'm trying to find out. I'm just a little bit unclear at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you. I joined the Army of Republika Srpska as a reserve officer and I did not interrupt my engagement in the military. By a decision of the ministry or somebody else's decision, I'm not sure who it was, there was vacancy for reserve officers to join the professional army if they fulfilled the conditions. I had to submit to a medical examination, submit my previous work history and so on, so officially I was accepted into the professional army in 1997 and this is where my salary is -- comes from. Up until 1997, I don't know after Dayton, from 1995, in 1996, we did receive some kind of compensation for our work but it wasn't all that much. So I did not leave my unit. I remained in the brigade and I'm in the brigade still now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after your removal from the position of commander of the 4th Detachment in 1992, where were you based? Where were you working from?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained in the battalion command -- no, the detachment command and then the battalion command. I stayed in the job of general affairs clerk. I first it was the detachment, then it was the battalion. So I remained in that same battalion in Samac until the 1st of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, of course the fact that you've come here to give evidence in this Tribunal, before the Trial Chamber here, would indicate that you support the work of the Tribunal, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, in supporting the work of the Tribunal, you would respect its judgements and any findings the Trial Chamber -- Trial Chambers or the Tribunal has made about things that actually occurred in the former Yugoslavia during the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, what is the point of asking this witness that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It goes to credibility but it will become obvious later on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't think it's fair to ask the way you phrased your question. I don't think it's fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can certainly rephrase it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, Mr. Pantelic asked you about the SDS yesterday. Have you ever been a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was never a member of the SDS or any other party. From 1990 onwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described yesterday when Mr. Pantelic asked you about the SDS, you described it as "a national party of the Serbian people." You remember saying that yesterday, just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember. That's how it is. This is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we proceed, Mr. Re I just wanted to say that we've noticed that Judge Lindholm is not with us. He's unable to come today because he's ill so we are continuing under Rule 15 bis (A). You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The SDS, which you describe as a national party of the Serbian people, that was a party that during the early 1990s, 1991, 1992, 1993, pursued a policy of ethnic separation by force. Now you're aware, before I go on, you're aware that three of its national leaders, that's Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Krsnik, and Mr. Karadzic have all been indicted by this Tribunal for committing war crimes in pursuance of SDS policies. You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know I know from television or from the press. Their work programme, particularly the programme of the SDS, was something that I didn't have the opportunity to read about or to deal with, and this doesn't sound to me as very good, ethnic cleansing. I don't understand that this was a part of their programme. I don't think that it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All I'm asking you is you're aware, aren't you, that the three of them, Plavsic, Krsnik and Karadzic have all been indicted by this Tribunal, whose work you told us you respect, for committing war crimes, you're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, you're aware that Mrs. Plavsic pleaded guilty last year and was sentenced several weeks ago for persecution, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that she admitted to some counts of the indictment and I know that later, she was charged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She admitted, sir, to pursuing -- she pleaded guilty to persecution based upon her involvement with the SDS, her leadership of the SDS, and its pursuing policies of ethnic separation by force, that is, ethnic cleansing in Bosnia in 1991, 1992, 1993. That's what she admitted and pleaded guilty to.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're aware, of course, that she was a very prominent SDS person, she was the president at one point of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're aware -- you of course were aware in 1992 and 1993 that the defendant, the accused Blagoje Simic, was also a member of the SDS and occupied a very high position in the SDS in the Bosanski Samac municipality, weren't you? I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your time as either commander of the 4th Detachment or afterwards, in 1992, and 1993, I think your evidence was in the last couple of days you were aware of the fact that non-Serbs were being arrested and detained in various facilities in Bosanski Samac and mistreated very badly by those who had detained them.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your time as the commander of the 4th Detachment and afterwards, in 1992, and 1993, did you ever visit any of the places where the prisoners were kept? The SUP, the TO, or the two schools?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the commander of the 4th Detachment for about a month or a day or so longer than that. I did not visit any of the prisons. I don't know what you call them. I didn't visit any of the TO staffs [As interpreted] or any other facility where detainees were being kept so I never visited them and I didn't see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was asking you about the SUP, the TO and the two schools. What about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Re, sorry to interrupt, actually this is a question to you, Mr. Re, not to Mr. Savic and I make sure I get your name right today and don't confuse you with Mr. Antic. Mr. Re, you are mentioning Mrs. Plavsic and her guilty plea and so on. You've mentioned a few times now war crimes. I'd like to be clear. I don't have the documents in front of me but did she plead to war crimes and crimes against humanity or only war crimes or only crimes against humanity? Because there is clearly a big difference in international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, is quite correct. If you give me one moment I'll pull out the judgement which is at my feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And maybe while we wait there is just one thing that we usually make this kind of correction in the transcript because I didn't visit any of the TO staffs. It's on page 6, line 25. Usually we refer to this in TO building so not to make any confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was -- I correct myself if I said war crimes. It was actually persecutions as a crime against humanity. I was using it in a fairly loose term but I will be very careful to correct myself in future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Obviously the reason for my question is that war crimes can only be committed during the context of an international armed conflict whereas crimes against humanity can be committed in international and internal armed conflicts which obviously is a point of contention in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But not in the other cases, many other cases, relating to the areas in the indictment to which Mrs. Plavsic pleaded guilty. There have been findings of an international armed conflict in those other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: But separate and apart from Mrs. Plavsic in the context of our case, if you're using the Mrs. Plavsic's guilty plea. I think we just have to be careful in the terminology of what we are asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I just go back to what I was asking you about a moment ago, Mr. Savic? And that was detention facilities. I was asking you about the SUP, the TO and the two schools. Now I'm going to ask you about the others. Did you ever visit detention facilities at Brcko, Batkovic or at the JNA barracks in Bijeljina in 1992 or 1993? And if you can answer it by saying yes or no, please do so.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During 1992 and 1993, in either your capacity as commander of the 4th Detachment or the work you were doing afterwards, did you ever witness any exchanges of civilians or prisoners between the Serb side and the other sides?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just need to correct you. I wasn't commander in 1992 and 1993. I wasn't a commander then. I was a commander for only a month or so in 1999. Until early June, I was the commander of the 4th Detachment. I didn't attend any exchanges ever, because it wasn't in my area of duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe something was lost in the translation. I understand you were a commander only up until June. The transcript to me says one thing you might have heard something slightly different but we'll move on from there. Did you ever witness any interrogations of prisoners where you were working in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Mr. Pisarevic asked you questions several days ago, you said that during the arrests in the first few days after the 16th, 17th of April, that some Serbs were arrested. Would you be able to help us out by telling us the names of these Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the names but I assume that those were errors. In our area you can tell by a person's first and last name in most cases whether they are Serbs Muslims or Croats so I assume that some people were arrested by mistake. The police was probably thinking those people weren't Serbs. A relative of mine, his name -- his last name was Ibralic, his first name was Davor or Damir, he was arrested by accident. He was a member of the detachment and his mother [Realtime transcript read in error "most"] is a close relative of mine. Her maiden name is Savic. I can't remember -- a name maybe termed purely Serbian in our area but I know about one or two cases where people were arrested by mistake. People were stopped in the street and arrested but I can't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one correction for the transcript on page 9, line 18, and his -- the witness said mother and here we read "most."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So apart from Mr. Ibralic, which has I assume a Muslim-sounding name, the best you can say is there were a few isolated incidents that you're aware of, of Serbs being arrested by mistake and the numbers were very small?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Isolated -- I think very few Serbs were isolated. I didn't know of that. I do know that there were Muslims and Croats. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your removal as the commander of the 4th Detachment -- sorry I'll withdraw that. I want to ask you about the meeting between the Crisis Staff and Colonel Djurdjevic on about 29th or so of May. In those few days around the May, 1992. Which you gave evidence about over the last few days. You spoke about a person called Aco Jankovic being present. Can you tell us who that person is, please?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that man. He's from Batkusa. I think he is a relative of Milan Simic and he was present there. I don't know what his role was there and then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was in the military at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. He was in a different unit. He was not a member of my detachment. Sometimes he was a police officer. I assume, but I'm not sure. He's from Batkusa. There was a unit there just like in Samac. Maybe he was a member of that unit but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether he was wearing -- whether he was in uniform at that meeting you attended with the Crisis Staff in late May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to say now what rank he held at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was a non-commissioned officer but I can't remember whether he was actually displaying his rank at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Vukovic, the paramilitary person who had put the gun in Mr. Zaric's mouth, was he present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question? Vukovic? I'm not sure who the person is. The man who put the gun into Simo's mouth, his name was Vuk. I didn't even realise what his first and last names were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man nicknamed Vuk, was the man nicknamed Vuk who Mr. Zaric told you had put a gun in his mouth, was he there at this meeting we are talking about at the moment?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that man. I didn't see him. I don't remember. I just heard that his name was Vuk. That was all. I didn't have any opportunity to see that person. At least not that I remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who he is or do you know what he looked like?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw him. I have no idea. I heard that he was a rather young man. I don't know, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Getting back to this meeting, Colonel Dencic wasn't there, was he?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one from the superior command was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your view, as a reserve officer of many years standing and your knowledge of Colonel Djurdjevic and serving with him was that -- was certainly not that he was too old to command the detachment, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe he had been born in 1940. I'm not sure, give or take a year or two I'm not really sure but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was in good health and of sound mind at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And respected by his subordinates? Not just because he was their commanding officer but because of his qualities as a soldier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that meeting, you knew that Mr. Simic, Blagoje Simic, was the President of the Crisis Staff, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric told you soon afterwards, within days, he travelled to Belgrade. You've given evidence of that. Were you aware that other members of the Crisis Staff, that was Mr. Tadic, Mr. Ninkovic and Mr. Todorovic also travelled to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe I have to object to this question. First of all, this witness testified about his knowledge of Mr. Zaric travel to Belgrade related to Crkvina massacre. And that's the only thing he testified about. I mean I have no problem but don't put this to the witness, the things that he didn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand the objection. Maybe I've missed something in the transcript. I haven't finished the question and I don't know what the objection is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe could be that -- I apologise because your question was, Mr. Zaric told you soon afterwards, within days he travelled to Belgrade you've given evidence of that yes and the witness gave evidence about his knowledge of Simo Zaric travelling to Belgrade in respect to the event that happened in Crkvina but then the other part of the question was that other members of the Crisis Staff -- first of all Mr. Zaric was not a member of Crisis Staff which was not in dispute here so I have a bit problem with this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think the problem is that it was combined with the other information. Split your questions and if you put a statement to the witness, let the witness answer first and then you go ahead with other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll do that I'm sorry about the word "other." I understand the objection to the word "other."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, after this meeting, several days later, Mr. Zaric travelled to Belgrade and you're aware that -- you've given evidence that he travelled to Belgrade several days afterwards, that's late May, early June?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, again, I apologise. Again, I believe that my learned colleague is mixing two things. Mr. Zaric did travel to Belgrade and the witness was testifying it was question by Mr. Pantelic and Mr. Pisarevic also that he travelled to Belgrade in relation -- well, actually that he was sent in Belgrade by Commander Nikolic to inform about the massacre in Crkvina. This is what the witness was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This was on May 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think more than that was in the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If I've confused what the witness has said, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Mr. -- I can clarify this. Did Mr. Zaric tell you he travelled to Belgrade in early May or late May, early June?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday, I don't know whose question it was, that Simo Zaric told us about what happened, what had happened at Crkvina. He spoke to his superior there and he said that he was on his way to Pelagicevo but then he phoned me from Pelagicevo and told me, Savic, Commander, I'm going to Belgrade, on official duty. I have some tasks to carry out there. Once I'm back I'll get in touch with you. That was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll put it another way. Are you aware, or did Mr. Zaric tell you that he had travelled to Belgrade after the meeting on about the 29th of May with the Crisis Staff, had travelled to Belgrade with members of the Crisis Staff and had met Mr. Bogdanovic in Belgrade? Were you aware of that or did Mr. Zaric tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a moment, please. This is not an objection to the line of questioning but for the second time in a row, the Prosecutor refers to a meeting of the Crisis Staff. The witness did give testimony yesterday of that meeting and who exactly was present so I would like to have this question rephrased. This was not a meeting of the Crisis Staff. Some members of the Crisis Staff were there and some weren't. Maybe on the premises of the Crisis Staff, just to specify when the question is asked about the meeting with Mr. Djurdjevic so this is the second time in a row. But I have no objections of a more general nature to the line of questioning. I just want this to be made clear we are talking about the premises of the Crisis Staff and not about a meeting of the Crisis Staff. My client was a member of the Crisis Staff, for example, but he was not physically present at that meeting. That's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you understand the objection, that this was not one of the formal meetings of the Crisis Staff because not all members of the Crisis Staff were present. It was a meeting, some members of the Crisis Staff were present on the premises of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly understand that but I don't think for the purposes of the question the witness was at all confused because he went to a meeting with some people of the Crisis Staff, although it was just a shorthand way of directing it, but if my friends want me to be as specific as I can be about who was there it will take longer but I can do it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, that meeting which was not a member -- a meeting of the Crisis staff as such but at which some members of the Crisis Staff were present, were you aware that Mr. Zaric a few days after that travelled to Belgrade with some members of the Crisis Staff, Mr. Simic, Mr. Tadic, Mr. Ninkovic, Mr. Todorovic, and met Mr. Bogdanovic in Belgrade? Were you aware of those details?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I have no idea who went and who travelled with whom and where they went. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of Mr. Zaric going to Belgrade several days after the meeting with some members of the Crisis Staff at which Colonel Djurdjevic told you he had been dismissed?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think your question is clear. Please, if I may just ask you, don't ask me about specific dates. It really was a long time ago the whole thing and when I came here to testify I told Mr. Pisarevic not to try to tie me down to any specific dates because really, I am doing my best to forget the whole thing and leave it behind. I want to keep the whole thing away. And that's why I may have forgotten some dates. Now, as to when exactly Zaric went to Belgrade, I don't know. Maybe he went several times. I know that he did go after the massacre at Crkvina but that's all I know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just excuse me for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, please don't think for a second I'm trying to tie you down to specific dates from 11 years ago. We understand completely how human memory works. Just within days, please just do as best as you can. Now, this is a more general question I'm going to ask you. When you signed that -- I'm sorry, you've given evidence of signing that letter with the 12 other commanders in about November, December, 1992, in which you severely criticised, that is you collectively, severely criticised what had happened in Bosanski Samac, especially by the paramilitaries or specials, after the 17 -- 16th, 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may say, those were not commanders. Those were members of the command. There is an essential distinction between those. So those were members of the command, not commanders. And I signed that too. I found myself in agreement with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will correct myself. When I said commanders, I -- it was a slip of the tongue. I did mean other members of the command. What came from that document was that the command, the members of the command, had disagreed with many of the actions of the Crisis Staff and its leadership following the 17th of April, 1992. That's a fair summation, just in terms of the -- of going through the disagreement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My signature meant what Commander Beronja's signature meant and the signature of other members of the command, what that meant was that the document was accepted in its entirety by Commander Beronja, by myself and other members of the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Re, just to lessen the confusion, could we just have the exhibit number of the document being discussed?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: P127, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and the other members of the command had grave concerns about the arrests, the rounding up of non-Serbs, the torturing of non-Serbs in detention facilities, the isolation of non-Serbs, and the actions of the Crisis Staff. That's a fair summary, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you had seen, those people were pursuing policies against the non-Serbs that could only be described as discriminatory, that is arresting them, detaining them, torturing them because they were non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that discrimination which you saw and heard about in Bosanski Samac after the 17th by the people you criticised in that document, P127, could really only be described as persecution against those non-Serbs in that period, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, before the 17th of April, 1992, as a long-time resident of the Samac municipality, you know that Serbs were less than 50 per cent of the population of the then Bosanski Samac municipality, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in a situation to be familiar with the exact percentage, but it strikes me as possible that Serbs were less than 50 per cent, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you know, they certainly weren't in a commanding majority, as in 60, 70, 80, 90, 95 per cent Serb?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I can say you're certainly right, yes. I think about 50 per cent but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a takeover with -- I withdraw that. Of course, before the 17th of April, 1992, the municipality of Bosanski Samac was multi-ethnic and had been democratically elected by the electors of the Bosanski Samac municipality in free elections in October, 1990, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the 17th of April, 1992, that democratically elected municipality government was no longer in force because its function had been taken over by the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That in effect of course was a takeover by one ethnicity, that's the Serbs, at the expense of the non-Serbs who could no longer participate in the government of Bosanski Samac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The takeover by one ethnicity at the expense of the others and you described in P127, that's the document with the 13 signatures on it including your own about the discriminatory policies put in place, such a takeover would not cause -- sorry, would cause interethnic conflict, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if the non-Serbs, as you've agreed, were actually in a majority, the takeover could hardly be seen as a liberation, could it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In our area, in daily correspondence, liberation is a word that has become a colloquialism, a word we tend to use frequently, and that's that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. -- you've already said that you disagreed with the actions of Dr. Simic and his support for the actions of the -- his and the Crisis Staff's or War Presidency's support for the actions of the paramilitaries following the events of the 17th of April. You agree with that? That's what you've said. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown 116 ter?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you're getting that, while these are being given to you, Mr. Savic, you said liberation is a word used colloquially but it has -- when it's used it has -- it's used in a very positive sense, isn't it? Just concentrate on me for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And people who use it, Mr. Savic, just bear with me for a moment, I'll come to the document in a moment, I'll come to that document in one moment, the word "liberation" is normally used in a military context in meaning the freeing of people from oppression, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "liberation" means the freeing of territory that has been taken by the enemy. It's a military term. Politicians often use the term, especially lately, during their electoral campaign. It's a catch word. They think they will garner more votes if they use the word often. Now, as far as the first meaning of the term is concerned, that's a true military term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: From that explanation by the witness, Mr. Re, it's no use pursuing this line of questioning on the meaning of the term liberation. It won't help us at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the -- from what you saw in 1992, 1993, and in particular in your observations of the work of the Crisis Staff and War Presidency, you would agree that the Crisis Staff had a significant role in working in the defence of the territory of Bosanski Samac, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the Crisis Staff did and how much it did, I really didn't know about. I did not have an insight into that. Your next question, when you say 1993, already in 1992 I was in Pelagicevo. I would go -- occasionally, I was told someone was arrested and taken away from their wives and so and so forth. I don't think the Crisis Staff knew everything about the work of the police, at least that's what I believe that they didn't know everything about the work of the police. I did not delve too deep into that. That's merely my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The word "paramilitary" is used -- has been used in these proceedings. It's been used in documents which are in evidence here. A paramilitary, could we agree on, say, a working definition from your perspective of a paramilitary formation being a group of armed people under a command, who are not within legitimate or formal government structures?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the military. Each member or a group, if they are in the part of any formational unit, then it's a -- and they are not members of the army, that's a paramilitary group. If any person is a member of the police but they are not a regular member of the police, then they are under the command of the police. This is how I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your understanding, the term paramilitary, a group of paramilitaries could be -- it could be a small group or it could be a large group, it could be a group of several people, it could be a group of 10, 20, 50, 100 people?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. Everything is possible. Everything that is not part of the formation is a paramilitary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I have an intervention in the transcript, this is page 21, line 13, 14, we heard that the witness said, "If a group is not under the command of the police, then it's parapolice." The way the sentence has been recorded in the transcript, doesn't make too much sense. So I would ask my learned friend to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It actually looks like lines 18 and 19 on the big monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think you can just ask the witness to go over the answer which he gave slowly so that the interpreters can pick every word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, I just want to clarify something from your last answer. The translation says if a person is a member of the police, but they are not under a -- not a regular member of the police, then they are under the command of the police. That is how I see it. Can you just -- if that isn't what you said, can you just please say it again and say what you did mean? Just that part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, as far as the military is concerned, everything that is not under the command of the military, whether it was a group of five or a larger group, for me, this is a paramilitary group, which is not under the command. I think that in the same way, as far as the police is concerned, if a police officer is not -- it's not known who is under the command, if he is out of anybody's direct control, then according to me, this is a parapoliceman. If his superior does not have any control over him, then he is not a police officer but a parapolice officer. This is at least what I think as far as the police is concerned. And as far as the military is concerned, this is something that I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The commandos or specials who came into Bosanski Samac in April, 1992, they were a paramilitary formation under your definition, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure that they were not in my unit and as far as I'm concerned, they are not soldiers. I think this is how they presented themselves, that they were specials, police officers, some of them would say that they -- he was a soldier. I know that in my unit, there wasn't a single member from that group that came to Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you could see, they were a paramilitary formation that had entered the municipality for whatever reason?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, this is the paramilitary and the parapolice, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they entered the -- entered it and after the takeover, they carried out, according to P127, which is the document with signatures on it, a campaign of -- a campaign of terror against innocent people in the town, that is the non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the way they did it, and from what you saw and from what you've said in that document, P127, you could conclude that they entered the municipality in order to carry out this organised campaign of terror against the innocent non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have no problem with the question truly but I think it would be fair to the witness to have the document P127. I really don't see the reason why my colleague hasn't given him this document. This is not actually a test or something whether he remembers parts of the document. I believe that it will be fair for him to have this document in front of him so when you're referring to some part of document or something like that, just it would be fair to the witness to take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The witness should be given the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not referring to P127, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You are no longer going to refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not referring to P127 at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, line 20, line 25, page 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not referring to P127. I'm referring to what the witness said in P127. I'm talking about something else altogether. The fact that I've mentioned P127 so that it's on the transcript as a reference point back to what the witness had earlier said doesn't mean that I'm actually referring to that at the moment. It's just for the clarity of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There is no harm in giving the witness the document, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Madam usher? Can the witness have the document in front of him?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: P127, sir, is the document which you signed with the other 12 members of the command and that's the one where you have drawn together your conclusions about or drawn together your opinions about what the paramilitaries or the specials or commandos were doing after the 17th of April, 1992. Just to be clear that that was something I was referring to in passing. You've got it there. My question was: I was asking you about the organised -- you agree that there was an organised campaign of terror or had to have been organised and then I asked you from what you saw and what you have recorded in that document, you could conclude that this paramilitary formation had in fact entered the municipality in order to carry out that organised campaign of terror against the innocent population. That's the non-Serbs. Couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown P89 ter?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just read the first paragraph of P89 ter, please, which is headed or which is a document which is called the decision of the introduction of the state of emergency on the territory of the municipality. I'm just going to read that paragraph slowly. It says, "Considering the difficult situation on the territory of the municipality, particularly in the town of Bosanski Samac, where a paramilitary formation entered the municipality in order to carry out an organised campaign of terror, against the innocent population in the town, and its surrounding area, the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac municipality made a decision on the introduction of a state of emergency on the territory of the municipality." Now that's on the 19th of April, 1992. You see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff, of course, was not referring to the paramilitary formation that you just agreed with me had entered the municipality in order to carry out this organised campaign of terror, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably. I don't know what the Crisis Staff thought but I can see what they wrote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've finished with that document. Thank you. Sir, you gave evidence over the last couple of days about the takeover and the events of the 17th of April, 1992, and I think you said people gathered or members of the detachment gathered at about 6.00 a.m. the next morning, around 6.00 a.m. You couldn't be precise on times, of course, it being so long ago and you said Mr. Zaric was there?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said Mr. Zaric and Mr. Antic came later. No, no. Excuse me. At 6.00 -- I came at about 3.00 or quarter past 3.00 a.m. on the 16th. Simo Zaric came later. If this is what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was referring to the later one at about 6.00 a.m. You said there were two. There was one at 3.00 and there was a later one in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were already in Pelagicevo at the time, Simo Zaric and Radovan Antic. I think I said that, if I remember it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 26, on line 13, it was 3.00 a.m. On the 16th. This is what we read in the transcript and it's obviously a slip of tongue so --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you said the 16th, you meant the 17th, didn't you? You said a quarter past 3.00 on the 16th. You actually meant the 17th, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that night, after you woke up and went to the command, Mr. Zaric went to Pelagicevo, did you see Mr. Tadic that night?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Zaric -- no, Tadic wasn't there then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the first time after you heard the firing of weapons in the early hours of the 17th that you saw Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he came in the afternoon, and I remember that Antic, Radovan, ordered him to transfer the command to prepare the work of the kitchen, to engage the quartermaster department, and this is what he worked on. I know that he was also obliged to check the issuance of weapons, to present the lists to the TO headquarters warehouse. This is what I remember. I don't know what the timings were.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak closer to the microphone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, could you please draw your chair nearer the microphones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, Mr. Pantelic asked you yesterday about the preparations that -- the preparations of the 4th Detachment for the town's defence around April, 1992. And your evidence was that there was a small unit of people involved in that. How many people were in this small unit involved in the preparation for the town's defence? I'm sorry, in preparing for the town's defence?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you are thinking of. I think that we are talking about the patrols that we had. There were about five or six patrols of mixed composition, of three members each, whose task it was, and the tasks were issued by the commander of the detachment, and also by myself when the commander wasn't there, just to observe everything that is out of the ordinary in town, they were obliged to report about, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you about specifically is an answer you gave to Mr. Pantelic where he asked you about preparation for the town's defence in a timely manner. It's at page 62 of yesterday's transcript, and you said, "We did have a small unit that was involved in such tasks." What I'm just trying to find out is how many people were involved in the task of preparing for the town's defence in a timely manner. Is it two, three, four, five? Whatever?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're thinking of the patrols, there were about five or six patrols numbering three members each so it was around 20 people, if you're thinking of the patrols. Before the outbreak of the conflict. They were already engaged from -- as of February. So it was their daily activity to walk around to see if there was anything unusual, and if there was something unusual, they were to report about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is your evidence that the planning or preparation for the town's defence was limited to these patrols, the five or six patrols of three members, around 20 people, walking around the town at different times of the day or night?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from that, it's apparent that there was no -- the 4th Detachment didn't see any major threat to the town's defences in April, 1992, because it only had several groups of three people patrolling the town?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment had information that Muslim forces, which were well armed, and Croatian forces, as you say, regarding the preparation and the way we did that, we thought that in the beginning, it was enough to just conduct this observation, and all that we did was done in accordance with the commands of the 17th Tactical Group. On the 17th, in the morning, we had a couple of these people who had arrived, these groups, a couple of them, and we started to call up the people and so on to see what was happening. They were also coming by themselves. It was maybe about 6.00 in the morning, and at that point we had about 50 people, and then these numbers grew later. That's how it developed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the 17th. I'm asking you about the period leading up to the 17th, and you've said that the preparation and planning was limited to patrols of two or three people, groups of maybe five or six of those. Now, were they patrolling the town at the same time or were they doing it in shifts, that is, two or three on and then two or three off? How did it work?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their tasks were issued by Commander Antic. At some point two were engaged, sometimes there were three patrols engaged. I don't know. This is something that he would know. He was the one who issued their tasks. When he wasn't there, then I was in charge of that. I know that Radovan was there for a day or two and then I was there or somebody else on duty from the command would be dealing with this, and the reports would be sent back. I don't understand you, in a way, these preparations. Preparations. Besides the patrols that we had, we also had weapons issued to us, not all of us, but people were arriving later and so on and so forth. This also was a form of preparation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, please confine yourself only to before the 17th of April. Are you saying that as far as you're aware, in your role as deputy commander, in April -- March and up to the 17th of April, 1992, there were no more, as far as you are aware, of no more than three patrols of two or three people patrolling the town or the municipality at the one time?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were five or six. This would occasionally change. The composition also of the personnel changed. I don't know what else I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there -- on the nights of March and leading up to the 17th of April, 1992, generally, as a rule, how many patrols did the 4th Detachment have doing the rounds of Bosanski Samac and the municipality? That's each night. Was it one? Was it two?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five or six. I think that's how much it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have silence from the counsel's bench, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on the night of the 16th -- withdraw that. The 4th Detachment, you've already given evidence, was part of the 17th Tactical Group, and was part of the JNA in April, 1992, leading up to the 17th of April, 1992. You agree that's the evidence you've given?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment was constantly under the command of the 17th Tactical Group and part of the JNA, not only up to the 17th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the night of the 16th of April, 1992, was the 4th Detachment -- were the only JNA soldiers in Bosanski Samac members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th of April -- could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the only soldiers, JNA soldiers, in Bosanski Samac, on duty, on the 16th of April, 1992, that's the night of the 16th of April, 1992, from the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the patrols, those patrols, the only ones. The members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you know, there were no other JNA soldiers on duty in Bosanski Samac on the night of the 16th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The 16th of April was the same as the previous days. Nothing in particular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many patrols, if any, did you -- did the 4th Detachment have patrolling Bosanski Samac on the night of the 16th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same as the previous days. I think that there were no increases. It was the same as the previous days. It wasn't more or less. I don't know whether it was four, five, six but it was the same. Their tasks on the 16th were the same as those on the previous days. Nothing in particular was different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was no shelling from Croatia, the Croatian side, until after the takeover on the 17th of April, was there?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the shellings -- shelling started first when commander Radovan deployed the people towards the Sava and Bosna rivers. One of the people was injured, wounded right away. After that, the shelling ensued and I heard the explosions for the first time and I understood that shelling was unpleasant, that this was a settled area, inhabited area, that buildings were damaged and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that wasn't my question, sir. My question was: There was no shelling from Croatia, that's across the Sava River, until after the takeover on the 17th of April, 1992, was there?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no shelling in Samac before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of your 4th Detachment members sent for training in the Serb Krajina in Croatia with the paramilitary forces who came to Samac before April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're aware of some local men from Batkusa going to the Serb Krajina in Croatia for training with those paramilitaries or commandos, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that some men left the area of the municipality. I know from my village, a couple of them were in that group, but there were people from Batkusa or Obudovac. We heard that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will take our break and continue at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, before the break I was just asking you about the people who went from Batkusa or other villages to train with the paramilitaries in the Serb -- in the Krajina, Serb Krajina, in Croatia. Were any of these people, to your knowledge, members of the 1st Detachment or 2nd Detachment, that is the men who went to train?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where they were deployed exactly, I don't know but it's possible that they were in their own units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These men who went for training, they were Serbs, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they came from Serb villages in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A takeover such as that which occurred on the 17th of April, 1992, required some preplanning, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can ask him a number of questions leading up to his expertise as a military person, in the reserve for X number of years, his subsequent experience as a full time officer in the VRS for the last ten years, his knowledge of military procedure, battle plans, what he was doing during the war, and -- getting to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re, only to a very limited point. This witness is a fact witness. And he has not given evidence that he was one of the people who were involved in the takeover so you can't ask him about the -- whether or not it required planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm asking him on the basis of he was a person, a deputy commander of the 4th Detachment, the next day, he was in the town. He was there, he knew exactly what -- he knew what was happening he was receiving orders or not receiving orders. He was aware of the paramilitaries, where they were from, what they were doing, which vital facilities in the town were being seized. It's a conclusion in my submission this witness must be able to draw from the things he saw, that is the facts that he observed in Bosanski Samac on the 17th. I was asking the shorthand way but I could take him through each of those things and come to the same point, a conclusion he as a deputy commander would have to draw from what he saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, from the facts -- from the facts known to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, you heard what I -- the exchange between Their Honours and myself about what you saw. Now, from your experience and what you saw on the 17th of April, that is the paramilitaries, the seizing of the vital facilities, the orders you received or didn't receive, it was apparent -- you could only draw the conclusion that the takeover by the paramilitaries was, and of course their arrival in Batkusa in the week preceding, their training and so on, you could only draw the conclusion from that that the attack had to be preplanned, couldn't you? As an experienced military officer, aware of military tactics, strategy and planning.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you that I simply didn't know what the plan of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Samac was. I didn't see any of that. I didn't take part in that group. On the 17th and on the 18th, the commander told me to stay -- ordered me to stay at the command for the whole time. Therefore, I only heard about what had happened. The intentions of our detachment and as far as our plans as you say were concerned, we only had to bring manpower levels up, get infantry weapons and await further instructions and orders. That was the intention and the conviction of our detachment, to prevent the spill over of war from Croatia into Bosnia by the HVO and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just excuse me? I just need to look at the transcript for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what I was asking you was, as someone who was there on the day and from what you observed of what the paramilitaries do, I didn't ask you about the Crisis Staff nor any connection with them, just in military terms, you agree that a takeover of the facilities in the town, in the way that it was done would have required preplanning by those who did the taking over? It wasn't spontaneous, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't our plan. It was not the plan of the 4th Detachment. Must have been someone else who planned it and who it was I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm just trying to get you to agree with me is there must have been planning by someone for it to have occurred in the way in which you observed it. I'm not saying the 4th Detachment did it. Whoever did it, must have preplanned it. That's all I'm asking you about. Because the degree of organisation and the way it was carried out would lead to you conclude as a military person that there must have been a degree of preplanning involved. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, again objection. I mean, it is multi-barrelled question. It's very general in nature. I believe it's confusing the witness with -- maybe my learned friend could be more specific. To ask this witness what is his personal knowledge about a plan issued by certain organ or certain person in Samac on that day at that time, otherwise he's trying to elicit an answer for a general question which cannot be held for this proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Pantelic, the question of counsel is quite clear and the witness can answer that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You followed the question? Based on your observations of what you saw, the degree of planning -- sorry, the way it was carried out, I'm not saying the 4th Detachment did it, I'm just suggesting that as a military officer there on the ground it was obvious to you, the only conclusion you could have drawn was that someone must have preplanned that attack which took over the town, whether you know who it was or not?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's possible that there was a plan but I don't know of any plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Savic, I think this is a question of military strategy. When a group takes over a certain area, and takes over vital facilities, do they have to have information on where those vital facilities are? I think the gist of counsel's question seems to be based on your knowledge as a military person, as well as being a person on the ground, as a matter of military strategy would there have had to be a plan that these paramilitaries weren't just going to descend into Bosanski Samac and just do it, as Mr. Re said, spontaneously? So I think in case you perhaps were not fully understanding, I think that's the gist of Mr. Re's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Firstly, none of us knew that any group of commandos would be arriving. We had never been in touch with those people. Personally, I knew nothing about any of their plans, nor did any members of the command know about those. It's possible that there had been plans, it's just that I don't know this for a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nothing from what you saw being there on the 17th could have led you to conclude that this takeover by the paramilitaries was a spontaneous random act of people who just dropped in from no where, could it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume what it was. I can assume that someone had ordered them to come, that there was an agreement for them to come, that they were told what they should do. But please believe me, I don't know whether this was planned in advance or not. I personally did not see, nor did anyone from the command see, anything. We just heard that they stormed the SUP building, the municipal building, that they took a number of facilities and institutions. The memorial centre with the radio station we heard that they had entered the PIK factory premises and I can't remember whether any other buildings or institutions. We merely heard that. All of us who were present at the headquarters of the command at that time. How they did this, I really don't know. I did hear later on about what had happened but at that point, I didn't personally witness any of this. I didn't see it with my own eyes. I merely heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear later on about how the attack was planned or how it was carried out? And who from?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from two men who were part of a patrol. I heard that they had come for them to show them around, to point out the various buildings and facilities, just like that. And we only heard at a later stage that they had already entered the SUP building and the MUP building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You agreed earlier with me when I asked you some questions of the effect of the takeover by the Serbs, that is one ethnicity, was at the expense of the other Serbs who could no longer participate in the government of Bosanski Samac, was a discriminatory act. You've already agreed with that, earlier this morning. What that means is that the takeover which you saw by Serb forces over territory in which the Serbs were not a majority, was a forcible takeover on discriminatory or ethnic grounds, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the morning or -- on the night or the early hours of the morning of the 17th of April, 1992, when you and other members of the command of the 4th Detachment, that's Radovan Antic, found out about it, you of course and you've given evidence of this, went -- communicated straight away with your commanding officer in the 17th Tactical Group, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did so because you wanted to find out what the -- I withdraw that. You did that because you needed to know what the 17th Tactical Group's commanding officer wanted you to do. That is you, the 4th Detachment, which you've already said were the only soldiers, JNA soldiers, in Bosanski Samac. That's the reason why you called command called Nikolic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you gave evidence to Mr. Pantelic, I don't want to repeat it, but you agreed that the 17th Tactical Group and the 4th Detachment were of course much, much larger than the paramilitaries or commandos who were in Bosanski Samac on the night or early hours of 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your estimation of the number of paramilitaries, was it 30 or 50 or something like that? What number do you give?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The large numbers in the -- the thousands of armed troops in the 17th Tactical Group could have easily overwhelmed those 30 paramilitaries had they been so ordered to do, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, this part, if you're asking me about the territory of the 4th Detachment, I'll tell you but what the orders for the command were, for the brigade were, what orders the command gave to the brigade, I really don't know. To overwhelm a group of people like that would have entailed the use of armoured vehicles. The use of specially trained people for combat against such groups. That's what it would have entailed in my opinion. Destruction, casualties. It was a big question how many people from the HDZ and from the SDA were actually armed and how you could distinguish those groups. We really didn't know at the time. I think that would have been very difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, maybe there is a misunderstanding?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, it doesn't help us at all to start speculation as to what would have happened if they had planned it this or that way. We better stick to facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour I'm sticking to orders which the JNA did or didn't give on that night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. It's better to stick to the orders which they gave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Sir, the -- the orders that -- I withdraw that. From your knowledge of subordination and command and control in the JNA in 1992, Nikolic was subordinated to another officer in a higher corps. I think that was, was it Jankovic or was there someone in between?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Jankovic but I'm not sure. I'm not sure who his superior was. My level was up to the Tactical Group. That means up to Nikolic. Now, who he received orders from, whether Jankovic or one of the generals, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your knowledge of subordination and your position in the hierarchy in 1992 based upon that, you know that Nikolic would have had to have received orders from someone up the chain and on the night of the 17th of April, 199 -- or the morning of the 17th of April, 1992, the orders that Nikolic communicated to the 4th Detachment from the chain of command in the JNA were to do nothing to prevent the paramilitaries from continuing with their takeover of the town.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we contacted Nikolic and informed him about what had happened, he called Simo Zaric and Radovan Antic to come there immediately. I can assume who he had received orders. I really can't speculate about that, who ordered him for someone to come to Samac if that's what you had in mind but I'm not sure, please try to specify when you ask me questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to specify. I'm asking you about your knowledge of subordination and the way it worked in the JNA in April, 1992. That orders that Nikolic gave to you had to have come from further up the JNA hierarchy, the orders that Nikolic communicated to the 4th Detachment. Based on the way the army worked in April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Tactical Group, that level, an officer of the same level, according to his own assessment is authorised to make a decision. However, in times of war, he is faced with a situation where he has to take a decision on his own, with his assistants, or he informs the superior command, the higher commanding level, and appeals for assistants, help, advice, in relation to occurrences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The effect of the orders that Nikolic communicated to you and Mr. Antic as -- and Mr. Zaric as members of the command of the 4th Detachment was to allow the paramilitaries to continue to seize control of Bosanski Samac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never received any such order. He was as shocked as we were by the arrival of those paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll go back a step. Paramilitaries arrived, the command of the 4th Detachment contacted Nikolic; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nikolic sought orders from somewhere else in the JNA, higher up, as to what he should do, as to what orders he should give you and the ground; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he did. Sometimes he would make a decision on his own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether he got them from higher up or not, Nikolic communicated back to you, the command -- ordered the command of the 4th Detachment not to prevent the paramilitaries from taking over the town?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. Nikolic ordered the JNA, the 4th Detachment, to see -- to defend the perimeters of the town; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To be deployed along the perimeters of the town and nothing more and to prevent enemy forces from crossing the rivers Sava and Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nikolic did not order, and he was the highest person who you or Antic spoke to, did not order you as the 4th Detachment and the only JNA soldiers in Bosanski Samac, to take action to prevent these paramilitaries from Serbia, the locals, from seizing control of the town, did he?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. He didn't order that, which means yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The paramilitaries were allowed by Nikolic order for to you do nothing, were allowed to continue their taking over of the town of Bosanski Samac by seizing the vital facilities, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the 4th Detachment were not entrusted with taking the town but rather the only task they received was to deploy themselves along the fringes of the perimeter of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nikolic's order for the 4th Detachment to do nothing to prevent -- non-order, put it in the negative, if you like, to prevent you, the 4th Detachment, from stopping the paramilitaries going about their business of taking over the town, in effect allowed them to continue doing it, didn't it? Because there was no interference from the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Because Nikolic told Radovan, "Leave this job to the organs of the civilian authorities and the civilian police." I clearly remember that. He told us not to interfere, that he would contact someone from the authorities and that that would be like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The effect of this was -- the effect of JNA non-action was to allow the paramilitaries and the civilian authorities to seize control of Bosanski Samac on an ethnic basis, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The effect of this was that it allowed the paramilitaries and the Serbs -- Serb police or whoever to install a Serb government, a Serb-only government, over a municipality that had a non-Serb majority; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the JNA's non--- sorry, inaction, the 4th Detachment's inaction, based upon Nikolic's order, allowed the Crisis Staff or the civilian authorities and the paramilitaries to consolidate their control over Bosanski Samac, over the next few days, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And everyone in the 4th Detachment command was aware that the effect of the JNA's inaction was that an ethnic-based takeover was allowed to occur in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I say everyone, I mean that's you, Mr. Antic, Mr. Zaric, Mr. Tadic, everyone who was in the 4th Detachment command, whether it's logistics, intelligence, the deputy commander, or the commander, everyone was aware of the effect of the JNA's ordered inaction, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, now the witness is really being asked to speculate as to what other people were aware of. I think the witness can only tell us about his own opinion but we can't really ask the witness to speculate as to what other people may or may not have been aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He has confined his question to the 4th Detachment -- the members of the 4th Detachment command. And that's -- as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, there is nothing wrong with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were dissatisfied with the way that this was done, and believe me, they did not have support with us, from the 4th Detachment, any national party, and even less the work being committed in this way, we didn't agree with that, but we didn't have any influence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just take you back to my question. My question was about the knowledge, the awareness. Everyone in the command of the 4th Detachment, and you've said people disagreed with what happened, that is you, Mr. Antic, Mr. Tadic, Mr. Zaric, and anyone else in the command was aware at that time that's April, 1992, that the effect of the JNA's inaction was to allow the installation of a new regime on discriminatory ethnic grounds?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that.
